newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Sandinista wants Nicaraguan election board to quit.
newsitem.headline: Sandinista wants Nicaraguan election board to quit.

text.p: A Sandinista leader on Monday called for the resignation of Nicaragua's highest electoral authorities following the disputed defeat of his brother in the Oct. 20 presidential elections.
Retired Gen. Humberto Ortega, brother of former president Daniel Ortega, said "incompetence" and "fraudulent actions" had put in doubt the victory of rightist Arnoldo Aleman.

"For the nation's stability, governability and the basic legitimacy of the new government of Arnoldo Aleman, it would be appropriate for all members of the Supreme Election Council to resign," he said in a paid announcement published in local newspapers.

President-elect Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance defeated Daniel Ortega of the left-wing Sandinista Front by 51 percent to 38 percent, but the Sandinistas charged the voting was fraudulent and riddled with irregularities.

The Sandinistas legally appealed against the results, demanding new voting in the departments (provinces) of Managua and Matagalpa, but their appeal was rejected late on Friday by the CSE, which has ultimate control of the electoral process.

Humberto Ortega, who was chief of Nicaragua's armed forces for more than 15 years before retiring in 1995, accused the CSE of being "politicized" and said resignation of its members was essential to restore credibility in democratic institutions.
Daniel Ortega has said his party will respect the "legality" of Aleman's government but not its "legitimacy."
CSE President Rosa Marina Zelaya on Monday played down Ortega's criticism, describing it as the opinion of one citizen among 4.2 million Nicaraguans.

"What we have heard is that his party has said that it is going to assume the seats in the National Assembly it won in the Oct. 20 elections. This is a recognition by the Sandinista Front of the electoral results," Zelaya told reporters.
During a bitter election campaign, the Sandinistas compared Aleman to hated former dictator Anastasio Somoza, who was ousted in the 1979 revolution, led in part by the Ortega brothers.

Aleman, in turn, warned of the return of the "dark night of Sandinismo." The Sandinistas governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990, fighting an eight-year war against U.S.-armed Contra rebels that left the economy in ruins.
